hmmt-feb-2011-algcomb-02.title: Checkerboard colouring
hmmt-feb-2011-algcomb-02.body:
Colour the desks like a checkerboard. Desks that are in front of, behind, or next to each other have different colours, and the desk grid is connected. The boys occupy $15$ desks, no two of them adjacent, and the girls occupy the other $15$ desks, no two adjacent. Along any chain of adjacent desks, genders must therefore alternate, so all boys sit on one colour and all girls on the other. There are $15$ desks of each colour.

There are $2$ ways to decide which gender gets which colour, $15!$ ways to seat the boys on their desks and $15!$ ways to seat the girls. The total is $2\cdot(15!)^2$.

(If the students of the same gender are regarded as indistinguishable, only the $2$ colourings remain; the official key accepted this reading as well.)

**Answer: $2\cdot(15!)^2$**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcomb-10.title: Parity strategy
hmmt-feb-2011-algcomb-10.body:
**$n$ odd, $n>1$.** There are $n-1$ moves, an even number, so Goliath makes the last move. The last move combines two numbers; Goliath can always make an even result (sum of two odds, product if at least one is even). So Goliath wins.

**$n$ even.** Work mod $2$. The board starts $1,0,1,0,\dots,1,0$. David first replaces the last pair $1,0$ by their sum $1$, giving a *good board*: alternating $1,0,1,\dots,0,1$ (odd length, starting and ending with $1$). Claim: after any move of Goliath on a good board, David can restore a good board (two numbers shorter). Goliath replaces an adjacent pair $\{1,0\}$ by $r\in\{1,0\}$ (sum $1$ or product $0$).
- If $r=1$: the new number is next to a $1$ (or is at the end next to a $1$); David combines them by *product* and gets $1$, which restores the alternating pattern.
- If $r=0$: it is next to a $0$ on one side (or at an end, next to a $1$); David combines it with that neighbour (by sum or product, giving $0$ for two zeros, or $1$ by sum for $0,1$) and the pattern is again alternating.

Since David makes the last move (the total number of moves $n-1$ is odd), the board ends as a good board of length $1$, namely $[1]$: odd, David wins.

So David wins exactly for even $n$. The $2011$th smallest even integer greater than $1$ is $2\cdot2011=4022$.

**Answer: 4022**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcomb-12.title: Harry wins for k <= 15
hmmt-feb-2011-algcomb-12.body:
Call an empty square *forbidden* if writing an $H$ there would create $HMM$ or $MMH$ horizontally or vertically. A horizontal run of $\ge2$ consecutive $M$'s in a row forbids at most the two squares at its ends, so the number of horizontally forbidden squares is at most the number of $M$'s, $k$. Likewise at most $k$ squares are vertically forbidden. Together with the $k$ occupied squares, at least $64-3k$ squares are safe for Harry. If $64-3k\ge k+1$, i.e. $k\le15$, Harry can place all $k+1$ letters safely and wins.

**Mike wins with $k=16$.** Put the $M$'s in four $2\times2$ blocks occupying rows $\{2,3\}$ and $\{6,7\}$ and columns $\{2,3\}$ and $\{6,7\}$. The horizontally forbidden squares are $(r,c)$ with $r\in\{2,3,6,7\}$, $c\in\{1,4,5,8\}$ ($16$ squares); the vertically forbidden ones are $r\in\{1,4,5,8\}$, $c\in\{2,3,6,7\}$ ($16$ squares), and these sets are disjoint. So $32$ squares are forbidden and $16$ are occupied, leaving only $16$ safe squares. Harry must write $17$ $H$'s, so some $H$ lands on a forbidden square and Mike wins.

The smallest such $k$ is $16$.

**Answer: 16**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcomb-14.title: Change of variables
hmmt-feb-2011-algcomb-14.body:
All numbers stay positive. Describe each pair $(x,y)$ by $[P,Q]=[xy,\ x/y]$. For the new pair, $x'y'=(x_iy_i)^2$ and $x'/y'=(x_j/y_j)^2$, so
$$[P_i,Q_i]\star[P_j,Q_j]=[P_i^2,\ Q_j^2].$$
Only the left $P$ and the right $Q$ survive, and each is squared. There are $1005$ pairs, so $1004$ merges. Think of the merges as a full binary tree whose leaves are the $1005$ original pairs in order. If the leftmost pair takes part in $k$ merges (depth $k$ of the leftmost leaf) and the rightmost in $n$ merges, the final pair is
$$[P,Q]=\bigl[4022^{2^k},\ (1007/1006)^{2^n}\bigr],$$
and different $(k,n)$ give different $(x,y)$ (since $4022>1$ and $\tfrac{1007}{1006}>1$). So we count the achievable $(k,n)$.

**Which $(k,n)$ occur?** Both $k,n\ge1$. The left spine of the tree has $k$ merge-nodes and the right spine has $n$, sharing only the last (root) merge, so $k+n-1\le1004$, i.e. $k+n\le1005$. Counting leaves: the leftmost and rightmost leaf, plus one more subtree hanging off each spine node other than the root on either side, gives at least $k+n$ leaves, and any larger number of leaves can be absorbed by enlarging one of the hanging subtrees, as long as at least one hanging subtree exists. A hanging subtree exists unless $k=n=1$, in which case the root's two children are just the two end leaves, forcing only $2$ leaves in total. Since we have $1005>2$ leaves, $(1,1)$ is impossible, and every other pair with $k,n\ge1$, $k+n\le1005$ occurs.

The number of pairs with $k,n\ge1$, $k+n\le1005$ is $\binom{1005}{2}=504510$; removing $(1,1)$ leaves $504509$.

(Enumerating all bracketings by computer for $m=2,\dots,8$ pairs gives $1,2,5,9,14,20,27$ distinct results, which equals $\binom m2-1$ for $m\ge3$; this agrees with the count above.)

**Answer: 504509**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcomb-16.title: Missing value and repeated value
hmmt-feb-2011-algcomb-16.body:
Since $f$ takes exactly $2010$ distinct values on $2011$ inputs, exactly one element $n$ of $A$ is missed and exactly one value $m$ is taken twice (all other values once).

Because $f(x)\le x$: $f(1)=1$, and inductively $f(x)=x$ for $x\le m$. Also $2011$ can only be hit by $f(2011)$, and backwards: for $x>n$ one gets $f(x)=x$ (otherwise $x$ would be missed or hit later). Hence $m<n$ and only the inputs $m+1,\dots,n$ are not fixed.

So $f$ restricted to $\{m+1,\dots,n\}$ must take each value of $\{m,m+1,\dots,n-1\}$ exactly once (the value $m$ is the one that is hit a second time, since $f(m)=m$ already), i.e. it is a bijection $\sigma:\{m+1,\dots,n\}\to\{m,\dots,n-1\}$ with $\sigma(x)\le x$. Put $N=n-m$ and shift by $m$: we count bijections $v:\{1,\dots,N\}\to\{0,\dots,N-1\}$ with $v(j)\le j$. For $j<N$ the allowed set $\{0,\dots,j\}$ has $j+1$ values, of which $j-1$ are already used by earlier arguments, so there are $2$ choices; for $j=N$ the last value is forced. Hence there are $2^{\,N-1}=2^{\,n-m-1}$ such functions.

Summing:
$$\sum_{m=1}^{2010}\sum_{n=m+1}^{2011}2^{n-m-1}=\sum_{m=1}^{2010}\left(2^{2011-m}-1\right)=\left(2^{2011}-2\right)-2010=2^{2011}-2012.$$

**Answer: $2^{2011}-2012$**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcomb-18.title: Symmetry plus the tie case
hmmt-feb-2011-algcomb-18.body:
Let $x$ be the probability that Hermia is elected given that Lysander votes for her, and $y$ the probability given that he votes for the other neighbour. If everyone, Lysander included, votes uniformly at random, by rotational symmetry each member is elected with probability $\tfrac1n$, so
$$\tfrac12x+\tfrac12y=\tfrac1n.$$

Compute $y$: if Lysander does not vote for Hermia she gets at most one vote (from her other neighbour). The $n$ votes are shared among $n$ members, so the maximum is at least $1$; for Hermia to win she must tie for the maximum, so every member has exactly one vote. That happens only if all members vote in the same rotational direction: given Lysander's vote this has probability $\tfrac1{2^{n-1}}$. Then all $n$ members tie and Hermia is chosen with probability $\tfrac1n$. So $y=\dfrac1{n\,2^{n-1}}$.

Therefore $x=\dfrac2n-y=\dfrac{2^n-1}{n\,2^{n-1}}$. (Check $n=3$: $\tfrac7{12}$, which matches direct enumeration.)

**Answer: $\dfrac{2^n-1}{n\,2^{n-1}}$**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcomb-20.title: One swap is enough, and sometimes needed
hmmt-feb-2011-algcomb-20.body:
Call a grid *legal* if rows and columns increase. Say Bob's grid $G$ *beats* Alice's grid $B$ if two numbers in the same column of $B$ lie in the same row of $G$. If $B=G$, Bob does not beat it (two entries of one column of $G$ are never in one row of $G$).

**At least one swap may be needed.** Whatever grid $G$ Bob chooses, Alice may include $G$ itself among her grids, so $G$ cannot guarantee victory; Bob must swap at least once in that case.

**Bob's choice.** Let $A_0$ have row $j$ equal to $2011j-2010,\dots,2011j$, and for $1\le k\le2010$ let $A_k$ be $A_0$ with the numbers $2011k$ and $2011k+1$ (end of row $k$, start of row $k+1$) swapped; this is one legal swap.

*Claim:* for $G\in\{A_0,A_1,\dots,A_{2010}\}$ the only legal grid not beaten by $G$ is $G$ itself.

Proof for $A_0$. Suppose $B$ is legal and not beaten, so the $2011$ numbers of any row of $A_0$ lie in $2011$ distinct columns of $B$. The numbers $1,\dots,2011$ therefore occupy distinct columns of $B$. If they were not exactly the first row of $B$, let $m$ be the smallest number not in $B$'s first row; $m\le2011$, and $m$, as the smallest entry outside the first row, sits at the start of its row, hence in column $1$, the column of $1$. Contradiction. So $B$'s first row is $1,\dots,2011$; remove it and repeat for each row: $B=A_0$.

Proof for $A_k$. The same argument applies to the rows above row $k$ (taken from the top) and to the rows below row $k+1$ (taken from the bottom, working with the largest numbers), so $B$ agrees with $A_0$ and $A_k$ outside rows $k,k+1$. Let $w=2011k-2010$. Row $k$ of $A_k$ is $S=\{w,\dots,w+2009,w+2011\}$ and row $k+1$ is $T=\{w+2010,w+2012,\dots,w+4021\}$. In the $2\times2011$ block of $B$ every column must contain exactly one element of $S$ and one of $T$. The numbers $w,\dots,w+2009\in S$ cannot be in the same column, and any number in the lower row of the block has a smaller number above it in its column, so none of $w,\dots,w+2009$ is in the lower row. Hence they fill the first $2010$ places of the top row. The top row's last entry and the whole bottom row are filled from the rest; the largest number $w+4021$ is at the bottom right, and the remaining element of $S$, $w+2011$, must then be the last top entry. This is exactly $A_k$.

**Strategy.** Bob starts with $A_0$ and looks at Alice's $2010$ distinct grids. If $A_0$ is not among them, he wins with no swap (they are all different from $A_0$). If $A_0$ is among them, at most $2009$ of $A_1,\dots,A_{2010}$ are among them, so some $A_k$ is not; Bob swaps once to reach $A_k$ and beats all of Alice's grids by the claim. Thus one swap always suffices, and one may be needed.

**Answer: 1**
